Helen of Troy. The woman whose beauty inspired a thousand ships to sail for war, and whose abduction sparked the greatest conflict in Greek mythology.

Helen was the daughter of Zeus and Leda, sister to Clytemnestra, which made her half-divine and extraordinarily beautiful. She is remembered as the face that launched a thousand ships, for her beauty inspired the Greek armada to sail for Troy. Originally she was married to Menelaus, king of Sparta, but she was spirited away by Paris, prince of Troy. Under the influence of Aphrodite, who had promised him the most beautiful woman in the world, Paris took Helen to Troy.

Her absence from Sparta and the dishonor of her abduction became the justification for the entire ten-year Trojan War. For a decade, she remained in Troy, though accounts vary on whether she loved Paris or resented her captivity. After the city fell and Troy burned, Helen was returned to Menelaus. Whether she was honored as a prize of war or reconciled with her husband, her journey was bound to those who loved and claimed her. Menelaus, her husband, had his honor insulted by her taking. Paris, the Trojan prince, took her to Troy under Aphrodite's influence. Her sister Clytemnestra shared the royal bloodline of Sparta and would know her own suffering during the war. And Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior, died fighting for her sake.
